extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate students in functional analysis or PDEs
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of basic Hilbert-space concepts: inner products, induced norms, projections, Riesz representation, bilinear forms, variational formulations (Stampacchia, Lax–Milgram), orthonormal bases, and related criteria and theorems. Intended as a textbook chapter for learning and applying these foundational results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scalar product (inner product) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A scalar product (u,v) on a vector space H is a bilinear form H × H → R that is symmetric ((u,v) = (v,u)), positive ((u,u) ≥ 0 for all u), and definite ((u,u) = 0 iff u = 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the fundamental algebraic structure; subsequent inequalities (Cauchy–Schwarz, parallelogram law) and induced norm properties follow from these axioms. The text notes bilinearity in both variables (real-valued setting) and highlights that the definiteness assumption is not needed for the elementary proof of Cauchy–Schwarz.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This inequality is a basic consequence of the inner-product axioms and is used to show that |u| := (u,u)^{1/2} defines a norm. The text also remarks the proof does not require the full definiteness hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Norm induced by inner product
rubrics_metrics.description: The quantity |u| = (u,u)^{1/2} is a norm; in particular it satisfies the triangle inequality |u+v| ≤ |u| + |v|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof using Cauchy–Schwarz; the notation |·| is often used for norms coming from scalar products. Many subsequent results assume this inner-product-induced norm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallelogram law
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used both as an identity valid in inner-product spaces and as a criterion: if a norm satisfies the parallelogram law, it arises from an inner product (Fréchet–von Neumann–Jordan theorem). The law is a central algebraic test for 'Hilbertness' of a norm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert space definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A Hilbert space is a vector space H equipped with a scalar product such that H is complete with respect to the induced norm |·|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completeness (Cauchy sequences converge) is required; many classical examples are L^2 spaces and Sobolev H^1. Much of the chapter's theorems assume H is a Hilbert space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform convexity of Hilbert spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Hilbert spaces are uniformly convex (Proposition 5.1), hence reflexive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given ε>0 and |u|,|v| ≤ 1 with |u−v|>ε, the parallelogram law gives a δ(ε)>0 so that |(u+v)/2| < 1−δ. The text sketches the quantitative relation and notes reflexivity follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection onto a nonempty closed convex set — existence & uniqueness
rubrics_metrics.description: For K ⊂ H nonempty, closed and convex and any f ∈ H there exists a unique u ∈ K with |f−u| = min_{v∈K} |f−v| (Theorem 5.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two proofs are given: one via reflexivity and lower semicontinuity/compactness arguments; another direct proof using a minimizing sequence and the parallelogram law to show it is Cauchy. The element u is denoted P_K f.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of projection by variational inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: The projection u = P_K f is characterized by u ∈ K and (f−u, v−u) ≤ 0 for all v ∈ K (Theorem 5.2, equation (3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalence between the minimization property and the inequality is proved by considering the one-parameter segment v_t=(1−t)u+tv and letting t→0. This characterization is used repeatedly (e.g., for cones and subspaces).

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection operator is nonexpansive (does not increase distances)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any closed convex K, |P_K f1 − P_K f2| ≤ |f1 − f2| for all f1, f2 ∈ H (Proposition 5.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the variational inequalities for each projection and adding them. This property is used to show contraction properties when composing with other maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthogonal projection onto a closed subspace
rubrics_metrics.description: If M ⊂ H is a closed linear subspace and u = P_M f then u ∈ M and (f−u, v) = 0 for all v ∈ M; furthermore P_M is linear (Corollary 5.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special case of projection onto convex set: one can test (f−u,v−u) ≤ 0 for all v∈M and deduce orthogonality. Linearity follows from this orthogonality condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riesz–Fréchet representation theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Every continuous linear functional φ on a Hilbert space H is of the form φ(u) = (f,u) for a unique f ∈ H, and ||f|| = ||φ|| (Theorem 5.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two proofs are presented: one using isometry into the dual and reflexivity/density, another direct construction via the orthogonal complement of the kernel. This theorem identifies H with its dual in a canonical way (with cautionary notes about embeddings when other spaces V are involved).

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution on identifying H and H*; pivot space triplet
rubrics_metrics.description: When V ⊂ H dense with its own Banach norm, there is a canonical embedding T : H* → V* (restriction). While H and H* can often be identified, one must not simultaneously identify V and V* without care (Remark 3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties of T: boundedness with a constant C, injectivity, and density of range in V* when V is reflexive. The text illustrates with sequence space examples showing differences between V, H, V*.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous and coercive bilinear form (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A bilinear form a : H × H → R is continuous if |a(u,v)| ≤ C |u| |v| for some C, and coercive if a(v,v) ≥ α |v|^2 for some α>0 (Section 5.3 definitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuity and coercivity constants C and α are explicit and used in existence/uniqueness theorems (Stampacchia, Lax–Milgram). Coercivity ensures injectivity and lower bounds on the associated operator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stampacchia theorem (variational inequality existence & uniqueness)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a(·,·) is continuous and coercive and K ⊂ H nonempty closed convex, then for every φ ∈ H* there exists a unique u ∈ K such that a(u, v−u) ≥ ⟨φ, v−u⟩ for all v ∈ K (Theorem 5.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a is symmetric, the variational inequality is equivalent to minimizing the convex functional (1/2) a(v,v) − ⟨φ,v⟩ over K. The proof uses Riesz representation and a contraction mapping argument on the projection operator with a suitable step ρ (choose 0<ρ<2α/C^2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lax–Milgram theorem (weak formulation existence & uniqueness)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a(·,·) is continuous and coercive on H and φ ∈ H*, then there exists a unique u ∈ H solving a(u,v) = ⟨φ,v⟩ for all v ∈ H (Corollary 5.8). If a is symmetric, u is the minimizer of (1/2) a(v,v) − ⟨φ,v⟩ over H.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the full-space version of Stampacchia with K=H. The theorem is central for solving linear elliptic PDEs via variational methods; the text notes the energy/least-action interpretation and alternative direct arguments showing A is bijective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operator A associated to a bilinear form and its properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Given continuous coercive a(·,·), there is a bounded linear operator A: H→H with a(u,v) = (Au, v) satisfying |Au| ≤ C|u| and (Au,u) ≥ α|u|^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These estimates are used to show injectivity, closed range, and density of range for A, leading to bijectivity. They also appear in the contraction estimate for fixed-point proofs (choice of ρ depending on α,C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Banach fixed-point theorem as a tool
rubrics_metrics.description: A strict contraction S on a complete metric space X (d(Sv1,Sv2) ≤ k d(v1,v2) with k<1) has a unique fixed point (Theorem 5.7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in the proof of Stampacchia by constructing S(v) = P_K(ρ f − ρ A v + v) and choosing ρ to make S contractive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert (orthogonal) sum and decomposition criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: H is the Hilbert sum H = ⊕_n E_n if the E_n are mutually orthogonal closed subspaces and their algebraic span is dense in H (Section 5.4). For u ∈ H, u = Σ u_n with u_n = P_{E_n} u and Σ |u_n|^2 = |u|^2 (Bessel–Parseval identity, Theorem 5.9).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theorem gives convergence of partial sums S_n = Σ_{k=1}^n u_k to u in norm, and the Parseval identity is fundamental in expansions and spectral decompositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthonormal basis definition and expansion / Parseval
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence (e_n) is an orthonormal basis if |e_n|=1, (e_m,e_n)=0 for m≠n, and their linear span is dense. Then every u ∈ H has expansion u = Σ (u,e_k) e_k and |u|^2 = Σ |(u,e_k)|^2 (Corollary 5.10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversely, any square-summable coefficient sequence (α_n) defines u ∈ H with (u,e_k)=α_k. The text warns the series need not be absolutely convergent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of orthonormal bases in separable Hilbert spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Every separable Hilbert space has a countable orthonormal basis (Theorem 5.11).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction via selecting a countable dense set and applying Gram–Schmidt / orthonormalization on nested finite-dimensional spans. This underlies the identification of separable Hilbert spaces with ℓ^2 up to isometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for a norm to be a Hilbert norm (various theorems)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several equivalent / sufficient criteria are given: (a) Fréchet–von Neumann–Jordan — parallelogram law implies arising from an inner product; (b) Kakutani — if every 2-D subspace has a projection operator of norm 1 (and dim E ≥3) then the norm is Hilbert; (c) de Figueiredo–Karlovitz — a Lipschitz property of the radial projection on the unit ball implies a Hilbert norm; (d) Lindenstrauss–Tzafriri — if every closed subspace has a complement then E is Hilbertizable (equivalent Hilbert norm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These give practical tests to decide whether a Banach norm comes from an inner product; the text gives statements and pointers to proofs/exercises and notes on the constants involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minty–Browder theorem for monotone operators (nonlinear extension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let E be reflexive and A : E → E* be continuous and strictly monotone ((Av1−Av2, v1−v2)>0 for v1≠v2) with (Av,v)/||v|| → ∞ as ||v||→∞. Then for every f ∈ E* there exists a unique u ∈ E solving Au = f (Theorem 5.16).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This theorem generalizes existence/uniqueness to certain nonlinear operators; references and further applications are given (Browder, Lions). It is presented as an extension of Lax–Milgram/Stampacchia ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carleson theorem on almost-everywhere convergence of Fourier series
rubrics_metrics.description: If u ∈ L^2(0,π) then the partial sums S_n of its Fourier series converge to u almost everywhere (Theorem 5.17).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This deep result is cited to contrast L^2 convergence (always true) with pointwise a.e. convergence; it explains why special orthonormal bases (sines/cosines) are particularly important.
